attribution.note: Marcus co-wrote this 2023 passage with Davis and explicitly re-endorses it here ('every word still holds true').

semantics.note: 'Far fewer' is a fair rendering of 'not nearly as many'. It is an observation, but its comparative clause has no defined reference set.

contract.note: The contract rightly finds that 'often claimed' and 'applications' have no corpus or unit. Scoring the comparison would mean choosing a baseline for the speaker. Treating it as not adjudicable is fair.

evidence.note: TheAgentCompany benchmark (Dec 2024): the top agent finished 24% of 175 tasks. This shows limits but counts neither practical applications nor what was claimed.

reviews.rationale: The first part, that some useful applications exist, could be tested. But the core claim compares against 'as often claimed', with no named claims, no unit for counting applications, and no reliability threshold. Any scoring would supply the comparison for the speaker. Not adjudicable as stated.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Naming Altman is grounded in the sentence before, which cites his blog post. Dropping 'try to' slightly softens the intent element, and the contract handles this by testing only omission.

contract.note: Requiring the same actor to change criteria is an ordinary reading of 'shift goalposts'. Reading 'duck' as observable omission is fair and does not demand proof of intent.

evidence.note: Altman's Reflections essay discusses building AGI without stating a definition, which supports the omission part. It does refer to a 'traditional' understanding.
OpenAI's Feb 2023 definition: earlier criteria existed. On its own it does not show those criteria changed.
Agüera y Arcas and Norvig set out explicit criteria. This does not show a change from their own earlier criteria.

reviews.rationale: The omission part holds: Altman's essay gives no definition (e1). The goalpost-shifting part is not shown: the packet has no dated sequence of one actor changing its criteria, because the charter and the profit-definition report were not used. The support condition needs both parts, and nothing contradicts either, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: A 2023 Marcus–Davis passage that Marcus explicitly re-endorsed in January 2025.

semantics.note: 'No doubt ... will' is an unqualified forecast with no deadline. The normalised proposition keeps all three predicted changes and 'somewhat'.

contract.note: Reading 'next generation' from the 2025 re-endorsement, and requiring only directional progress, is an ordinary and fair reading. The early-resolution rule asks for two model families and all three changes.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own disclosure for Claude 3.7 Sonnet (Feb 2025): capability gains, the Claude Code workflow, and 45% fewer unnecessary refusals.
OpenAI's own disclosure for GPT-5 (Aug 2025): better evaluations, broader agentic tool use, and about 45% fewer factual errors than GPT-4o.
Independent METR study (v1, Mar 2025): frontier task-completion time horizons keep growing through Claude 3.7 Sonnet.
METR trial: developers were 19% slower with early-2025 tools. This limits any universal productivity reading but does not contradict the narrow forecast.

reviews.rationale: The early-resolution rule is met. Two major families, Anthropic in Feb 2025 and OpenAI in Aug 2025, report greater abilities, expanded workflows, and measured cuts in existing weaknesses (refusals, factual errors). METR independently confirms the capability gains. The error reductions rest on company figures. e4 limits universal claims but not this modest forecast.

attribution.note: A Marcus–Davis passage that Marcus explicitly re-endorsed in this post.

semantics.note: The revised proposition matches the statement and no longer asserts that AGI was not achieved.

contract.note: Reading hyperbolic 'zero justification' as 'no adequate empirical basis under Marcus's stated definition' is an ordinary reading. Fixing the date to publication day is the evaluator's choice and is flagged.

evidence.note: The ARC evaluator says o3 is not AGI and fails easy tasks. This backs caution but is a single benchmark, not broad coverage.
o3's 87.5% on ARC-AGI-1 shows adaptation to novel tasks, but one benchmark does not meet Marcus's generality standard.
US/UK AISI testing of o1 found tool-calling problems, with findings limited to the version tested.
The 2023 Sparks paper argues early GPT-4 was incomplete AGI. It is earlier and uses a weaker standard, so it does not meet the contradiction condition.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows shortcomings: easy-task failures and reliability problems. But it does not broadly show that January 2025 systems lacked human-comparable flexibility and reliability, which the support condition requires. Nor does it show a system meeting Marcus's definition, which the contradiction condition requires. The packet itself admits this coverage gap. Unresolved.
